title: Airway
why_this_matters: When a dog cannot be intubated and cannot be oxygenated, delay to an emergency front-of-neck airway has been linked to deaths in a small case series; airway skill and timing are the issue, not species-specific anatomy alone [1][2].

what_changes_from_human.point: In five small-animal cannot-intubate, cannot-oxygenate cases (3 dogs, 2 cats) all died, and emergency front-of-neck airway access was late, not attempted or not possible in several; the authors argue for early recognition and a defined trigger [1].
Brachycephalic dogs in airway crisis who needed immediate intubation had 71% survival to discharge and a 48% complication rate; longer intubation time raised pneumonia risk [3].

recognition: In healthy anesthetized dogs, final-year students took a median 54 s to intubate versus 12 s for qualified veterinarians; the authors recommend a 55 s supervisor take-over limit and pre-oxygenation to limit hypoxemia [2]. This was an anesthesia setting, not a field emergency.
Brachycephalic obstructive airway syndrome in crisis can require immediate intubation; French Bulldogs regurgitated more often than other brachycephalic breeds [3].

management: Time-limited attempts and early escalation are the lesson from the CICO case series; the authors propose a guideline for emergency front-of-neck access [1].

takeaway: A dog that cannot be intubated needs a time limit and a plan to escalate early; get a veterinarian with airway skills involved fast.
